label: Who was the man whose track joined the horse's near Mapleton?
quote: A man’s track was visible beside the horse’s.

possibilities.value: the man who struck Straker down, following the horse

reasoning.text: Someone was in the hollow with Straker and the horse. The horse ran off, and that man may have followed it across the moor and caught it.
Simpson was out on the moor in the storm that night and had money against the favourite. He might have come upon the horse before he was arrested.
The track ends at Mapleton's gates, and a Mapleton groom runs out from them to keep strangers away.

label: Why did the man with the horse set off towards King's Pyland and then turn back?
quote: the same tracks coming back again in the opposite direction

possibilities.value: he meant to return the horse, then decided to keep it

reasoning.text: Leading a stray towards its own stable looks like returning it. Coming back the other way means he changed his mind, perhaps when he saw what keeping the favourite out of the race could be worth.

possibilities.value: he went that way for some other reason, such as to keep out of sight

reasoning.text: The turn towards King's Pyland may have been a detour rather than an attempt to bring the horse home.

label: What is it that Silas Brown promises shall be there?

reasoning.text: The horse's tracks led to Mapleton's gates. Brown came out of his talk with Holmes broken, and Holmes had told Ross to keep the horse entered for the Cup.

label: Where is it that Silas Brown promises it shall be?

possibilities.value: at the race for the Wessex Cup on Tuesday

reasoning.text: Holmes insisted that the favourite's name stay in the entries for the Cup (¶111).
If Brown has the horse, the plain thing to promise is to return it to its own stable.

label: What would Silas Brown change before it is there?
quote: Should I change it first or not?

possibilities.value: put its appearance back as it was, after it had been altered

reasoning.text: The police examined Mapleton and found nothing, yet the tracks went in at its gates. If it is the horse, it may have been altered so as not to be known, and 'change it' would mean undoing that.

possibilities.value: alter it in some way before handing it over

reasoning.text: 'Change it first' may mean doing something new to it before it is brought out.

value: the horse broke loose in the struggle and was taken up later by someone else

reasoning.text: The horse's track runs alone from the hollow side of the moor. A man's track joins it only near Mapleton, so nobody led the horse away from the killing.
